title: The Sharpe Pint: Hugging Nvidia, Gilt-Edged Headaches, and the Art of the Foot-in-the-Door

opening_mood.text: Grab a pint, pull up a chair, and let's unpack a Friday session that gave the markets a proper whipping. Just when everyone was looking forward to a quiet long weekend, the US macro machine decided to throw a massive spanner in the works. From central bank independence warnings in Threadneedle Street to a massive tech land-grab in Silicon Valley, we have had a wild 24 hours. Here is everything you need to know to look like the smartest person in the room on Monday morning.

content.text: 1. Nvidia Hugs the Face of Open Source for $12.9B

Nvidia has agreed to acquire Hugging Face, the absolute town square of open-source AI, for exactly $12,930,300,000. The price tag itself is a double Easter egg: '129303' is the decimal Unicode representation of the Hugging Face emoji (🤗), and it is also the exact hex colour code for Nvidia's signature green. Hugging Face hosts over 3 million models and serves 18 million developers, and Nvidia has promised to keep the platform open and compute-agnostic.

Why it matters: This is Nvidia's second-largest acquisition ever, and it is a masterclass in vertical integration. As hyperscalers try to escape Nvidia's eye-watering chip margins by building their own custom silicon, Nvidia is moving up the stack to capture the developer ecosystem. If you own the library where every open-source model is downloaded, evaluated, and fine-tuned, you can ensure that the default, most optimised path always runs best on Nvidia hardware.

The City angle: For asset managers and tech analysts, this is a massive platform play. It shifts the AI value chain from pure hardware to ecosystem lock-in. It also raises serious antitrust questions: can a hardware monopolist neutrally run the world's largest open-source software repository?

items: What to say at work: 'Jensen is playing 4D chess here. He doesn't need to force developers onto his chips; he just bought the front door of the open-source ecosystem and made sure the fastest path runs on Nvidia. It's a brilliant defensive play against custom silicon, but open-source neutrality is officially dead.'

content.text: 2. The US Jobs Report Shatters the 'Cooling' Narrative

August nonfarm payrolls surged by 162,000, absolutely obliterating the consensus forecast of 55,000. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, and July's scary negative print was revised away entirely into positive territory (+21,000). It was a massive upside surprise that caught the market completely off guard.

Why it matters: Just 24 hours earlier, Fed Governor Christopher Waller had sparked a relief rally by hinting the Fed would hold rates steady in September. This blowout print blew that narrative to pieces. Short-term Treasury yields surged, and the market's implied probability of a September rate hike jumped above 60%, reversing the 'hold' consensus in a matter of minutes.

items: What to say at work: 'Waller's dovish relief rally lasted all of twelve hours. With July's job losses revised away and August tripling expectations, the 'hold' camp is completely on the defensive. If CPI comes in hot next week, a September hike is a lock.'

content.text: 3. Broadcom's AI Boom Meets the 'Lofty Expectations' Curse

Broadcom reported Q3 FY2026 earnings, showing AI semiconductor revenue skyrocketed 221% year-over-year to $16.7 billion, driven by custom accelerators and networking chips. Yet, the stock fell over 5% in after-hours trading.

Why it matters: Broadcom is the quiet giant of the AI trade. It doesn't sell off-the-shelf GPUs like Nvidia; it co-designs custom application-specific integrated circuits (XPUs) for hyperscalers like Google, Meta, and OpenAI who want to escape Nvidia's margins. Despite bringing in $173 million in profit per day, its Q4 revenue guidance of $34.8 billion fell just short of the $35.05 billion Wall Street demanded.

items: What to say at work: 'Broadcom is minting cash faster than almost anyone in tech, co-designing OpenAI's custom chips, and yet the stock gets punished because guidance was off by a rounding error. It's a classic late-cycle valuation squeeze where perfection is already priced in.'

content.text: 4. Oil Prices Surge as the Iran War Escalates
Brent crude surged towards $96 a barrel and WTI held near $92, with both benchmarks posting weekly gains of 7% to 10%. US diesel prices hit an all-time high of $5.85 a gallon.

Why it matters: The six-month-old conflict with Iran has escalated sharply, with the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to commercial shipping. US and Israeli strikes have intensified, and Kuwait was recently hit, raising severe supply disruption fears.

The City angle: Energy is now the most immediate constraint on global growth and inflation. For macro funds and commodity desks, this is a massive stagflationary shock. Higher diesel prices feed directly into freight and delivery costs, meaning inflation is going to remain sticky just as central banks are debating rate hikes.

items: What to say at work: 'With the Strait of Hormuz effectively shut and diesel at nearly six dollars a gallon in the US, the inflation debate isn't over. It's going to be a very expensive winter for supply chains, and macro funds are piling back into energy longs.'

content.text: 5. UK Gilt Yields Hit Post-Financial Crisis Highs
The UK 10-year gilt yield rose to 5.21% and the 30-year yield reached 5.90%—its highest level since 1998—amid a global bond sell-off.

Why it matters: This is an immediate baptism of fire for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's new administration and Chancellor John Healey, who is preparing his first Budget for October 28. Higher yields mean the government's debt-servicing costs are ballooning, wiping out the fiscal headroom left by the previous administration.

The City angle: The Chancellor is severely constrained. He has pledged not to raise the main rates of personal taxation, but restoring the fiscal buffer will require finding roughly £10 billion a year in spending cuts or stealth taxes. For sterling and gilt traders, the October Budget is now a high-stakes event.

items: What to say at work: 'The bond vigilantes are back, and they've given the new Chancellor a £10 billion headache before he's even delivered his first Budget. With 30-year gilts yielding nearly 6%, John Healey has zero room to manoeuvre without triggering a Truss-style market tantrum.'

content.text: 6. Bank of England's Huw Pill Warns of 'Fiscal Dominance'

Bank of England Chief Economist Huw Pill warned that mounting fiscal pressures across major economies are sharply raising the risk of 'fiscal dominance'—where central banks face pressure to help finance government deficits rather than focus on inflation.

Why it matters: Pill's comments are a rare, blunt warning from a central banker about the erosion of institutional independence. They sit alongside his separate push for a Bank Rate rise to guard against Middle East-driven inflation risks.

items: What to say at work: 'When the Chief Economist of the Bank of England starts openly warning about 'fiscal dominance,' you know the adults in the room are getting worried. It's a polite way of saying governments are borrowing too much, and they're going to try and make the central bank pay for it.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The 'Good News is Terrible News' Friday

On Thursday, we had Fed Governor Christopher Waller playing the role of the ultimate dove, quoting John Lennon to tell markets to 'give disinflation a chance.' Yields tumbled, equities rallied, and everyone was looking forward to a quiet long weekend. Then Friday's nonfarm payrolls dropped, and the mood turned instantly sour.

The US economy added a massive 162,000 jobs in August, absolutely obliterating the consensus estimate of 53,000. To rub salt in the wounds of the rate-cut hopefuls, July's scary negative print was revised away into a positive 21,000 gain, and June was bumped up too. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1% despite a massive influx of people entering the labour force. It is the strongest hiring month since March, and it essentially tells the Fed that the US economy is far too resilient to justify sitting on its hands.

Within minutes of the release, the market's pricing for a rate hike at the September 15–16 FOMC meeting flipped from a coin-toss to over 60% probability. The Fed's current target rate of 3.5%–3.75% suddenly looks like it has further to climb, completely reversing the Waller-driven relief rally in a matter of hours.
The Geopolitical Diesel Shock

If a roaring labour market wasn't enough to keep the Fed hawkish, the geopolitical backdrop is actively pouring fuel on the fire. The six-month-old conflict between the US and Iran escalated dramatically this week, with retaliatory strikes hitting US bases across the Middle East and effectively shutting down the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping.

Brent crude ended the week up nearly 9%, hovering around $95.37 a barrel. But the real kicker is diesel. US diesel prices hit an all-time high of $5.85 a gallon on Friday. For anyone in asset management or macro, this is the ultimate supply-side headache. Diesel is the lifeblood of global logistics, shipping, and manufacturing. A spike here is a direct tax on corporate margins and a guaranteed way to keep headline inflation sticky.
The Cross-Asset Read: Where to Hide?

items: Equities: The S&P 500 slipped 0.4% to 7,718.60, the Dow fell 0.5% to 53,414.25, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq gave back 0.3% to 26,506.99. Interestingly, the small-cap Russell 2000 bucked the trend, gaining 0.2% to 2,975.65.

Fixed Income: The bond market got absolutely battered. The policy-sensitive 2-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.37%, while the benchmark 10-year yield marched up to 4.81%—approaching multi-year highs as investors demand a hefty term premium for inflation and deficit risks.

Commodities: Spot gold fell 1.3% to $4,420 per ounce. Given the massive backup in real yields, gold actually held up remarkably well, showing that geopolitical anxiety is keeping a solid floor under safe havens.

content.text: What the Market is Really Saying

Underneath the surface, the cross-asset action is telling us that the 'soft landing' narrative is being severely tested by a twin-shock of sticky domestic demand and geopolitical supply constraints. If you're prepping for an interview or a client meeting next week, the talking point is clear: the Fed is trapped. They want to pause to let the lagged effects of previous hikes work, but they can't ignore a job market that refuses to cool down, especially when energy-driven inflation is knocking at the door.

content.text: Unlevered vs Levered Free Cash Flow: The First Law of Valuation

Imagine you are buying a flat in London. The property generates £20,000 a year in rent. That £20,000 is the cash the asset produces, regardless of how you choose to fund it. If you buy it entirely with cash, that £20,000 is yours to keep. If you take out a massive mortgage, a chunk of that £20,000 goes straight to the bank in interest and principal repayments, leaving you with, say, £5,000. In corporate finance, this is the exact distinction between Unlevered Free Cash Flow (Free Cash Flow to Firm, or FCFF) and Levered Free Cash Flow (Free Cash Flow to Equity, or FCFE). It is one of those foundational concepts that separates the people who actually understand valuation from those who just memorised a few formulas to survive an interview.
The Definitions: Who Gets the Cash?

Unlevered Free Cash Flow (FCFF) is the cash generated by a company’s core operations before taking into account any debt payments. It represents the cash available to all capital providers—both the banks who lent the money and the shareholders who own the equity. Because it is capital-structure neutral, it lets you compare the operational efficiency of two businesses without getting distracted by how they are financed.

Levered Free Cash Flow (FCFE) is the cash left over after the company has met all of its financial obligations. This is the cash available only to equity shareholders. It is what is left after paying operating expenses, taxes, reinvesting in the business (CapEx and working capital), and paying the interest and principal on any debt.
Let’s Do the Maths (Without the Headache)
Let’s look at a quick hypothetical example. Imagine 'Pint & Co.', a high-end pub chain, has the following financial metrics:

items: EBIT (Operating Income): £100m
Tax Rate: 20%
CapEx: £20m
Working Capital Change: -£5m (an outflow)
Interest Expense: £10m
Net Debt Repayment: £12m (they paid down some debt)

content.text: To calculate Unlevered FCF (FCFF), we start with operating performance and ignore the debt:

items: EBIT * (1 - Tax Rate): £100m * (1 - 0.20) = £80m (this is NOPAT, or Net Operating Profit After Tax)
Add back D&A: £80m + £15m = £95m
Subtract CapEx: £95m - £20m = £75m
Subtract Working Capital Outflow: £75m - £5m = £70m
Result: Pint & Co. generated £70m of core unlevered cash.

content.text: To calculate Levered FCF (FCFE), we have to account for the debt. We can start with Net Income:

items: EBIT: £100m less £10m Interest = £90m EBT. After 20% tax, Net Income = £72m
Add back D&A: £72m + £15m = £87m
Subtract CapEx: £87m - £20m = £67m
Subtract Working Capital Outflow: £67m - £5m = £62m
Subtract Net Debt Repayment: £62m - £12m = £50m
Result: Only £50m is actually available to equity holders. The other £20m went to pay the tax-adjusted interest (£8m after-tax) and pay down the principal (£12m).

content.text: Notice how the bridge works perfectly: FCFE (£50m) = FCFF (£70m) - After-Tax Interest (£8m) - Net Debt Repayment (£12m).
Why This Matters in Asset Management
The legendary NYU Stern professor Aswath Damodaran has a 'First Law of Valuation': Never mix and match cash flows and discount rates. If you get this wrong, your valuation is instantly useless.

items: Unlevered FCF (FCFF) must be discounted using the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC). Because the cash flow belongs to both debt and equity holders, the discount rate must reflect the cost of both. This gives you the Enterprise Value (EV). To get to Equity Value, you then subtract Net Debt.

Levered FCF (FCFE) must be discounted using the Cost of Equity (Ke). Because this cash belongs solely to shareholders, the discount rate must only reflect the risk of the equity. This gives you the Equity Value directly.

content.text: Why do investment bankers and buy-side analysts almost always default to Unlevered FCF? Because capital structures change. If a company plans to aggressively pay down debt or issue new bonds, its interest expenses and net borrowing will swing wildly. This makes Levered FCF highly volatile and incredibly annoying to forecast. Unlevered FCF isolates the operating health of the business, independent of how it is funded. We only tend to use Levered FCF for financial institutions (where debt is an operating input, not just a funding source) or in highly leveraged transactions like LBOs where we want to track the exact cash available to pay down debt.
The Common Beginner Mistakes

items: The Mismatch Trap: Discounting Unlevered FCF with the Cost of Equity, or Levered FCF with WACC. If you do this in an interview or a model, you will be shown the door.

Double-Counting Interest: When building Levered FCF starting from Net Income, beginners often subtract interest expense again. Remember, Net Income is already net of interest. You do not need to subtract it twice.
Assuming CFO is Unlevered: On the Cash Flow Statement, Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) is actually a levered metric under US GAAP because it starts with Net Income (which has interest deducted).

content.text: How to Nail This in an Interview

"Unlevered FCF is the cash available to all capital providers before debt payments, while Levered FCF is the residual cash left for equity holders after debt service. Because of this, we discount Unlevered FCF by WACC to find Enterprise Value, and Levered FCF by the Cost of Equity to find Equity Value directly. We prefer Unlevered FCF in most DCFs because it isolates the operating performance and isn't distorted by changes in capital structure."
Over a Pint: What to Say at the Pub

"Everyone is raving about that tech firm's operating cash flow, but they are carrying a mountain of expensive private credit debt. If you actually run the numbers down to Levered FCF, the equity holders are getting absolutely squeezed. The core business is great, but the capital structure is eating all the lunch."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: The Latency Trap of Deep Learning

We all love deep learning. It's powerful, flexible, and makes for great slide decks. But in the real world of quantitative finance—whether you're fitting a volatility surface, pricing options, or running intraday return predictions—deep networks have a massive Achilles' heel: training latency. Waiting for backpropagation and gradient descent to converge is fine when you're training a model overnight, but if you need to update your pricing engine or risk models in real-time, it's about as useful as a delayed train on the District Line.

This is where the Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) comes in. It's a classic machine learning technique that has recently found a powerful second life in quantitative finance, offering a way to get the non-linear modeling power of neural networks at the speed of a simple linear regression.
The Idea: Neural Networks Without the Backprop

An Extreme Learning Machine is a single-hidden-layer feedforward neural network (SLFN) with a brilliant twist: you don't train the hidden layer. Instead, you randomly initialize the weights and biases of the hidden layer and freeze them forever. Because the hidden layer is fixed, the relationship between the hidden layer's outputs and the target variable is purely linear. This means you can solve for the output weights analytically in a single step using closed-form linear algebra (like Ridge regression or the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse).

By skipping backpropagation entirely, you turn a non-convex, iterative optimization problem into a simple, convex, one-step calculation. You get the non-linear feature mapping of a neural network, but you train it in milliseconds.
A Quick Python Implementation
Where This Wins in Finance

items: Real-Time Option Pricing: Learning parametric pricing functions for complex derivatives where analytical formulas don't exist, but standard neural networks are too slow to calibrate on the fly.
Implied Volatility Surface (IVS) Fitting: Rapidly completing and smoothing the volatility surface from sparse market data without arbitrage violations.

Solving PDEs: A super-fast alternative to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). Instead of training a PINN for thousands of epochs to solve the Black-Scholes PDE, an ELM can solve it almost instantly by matching the boundary conditions at the output layer.

content.text: The Paper Angle

In their paper, 'Fast Learning in Quantitative Finance with Extreme Learning Machine', researchers Liexin Cheng, Xue Cheng, and Shuaiqiang Liu put ELMs to the test across multiple financial tasks. They found that ELMs achieved comparable accuracy and superior generalization compared to deep neural networks and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), but at a fraction of the computational cost. Crucially, they demonstrated that ELMs could solve Black-Scholes-type PDEs with high precision while completely bypassing the slow, iterative training of standard PINNs.
The Interview & Pub Conversation Angle

If you're in an interview or chatting with colleagues about model latency, this is a fantastic concept to bring up. It shows you understand that practical engineering constraints (like execution speed and calibration time) are just as important as theoretical accuracy. You can frame it like this: 'Everyone is obsessed with deep learning, but in high-frequency trading or real-time risk management, latency is everything. If you can get 99% of the accuracy of a deep network in 0.1% of the time using an Extreme Learning Machine, that's a massive commercial win. It's essentially a non-linear feature generator followed by a ridge regression.'
The Catch

items: Dimension Scaling: Because the hidden weights are random and untrained, you typically need a larger number of hidden units (neurons) than a fully trained deep network to achieve the same level of representation power.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity: The model's performance is highly dependent on the choice of activation function and the L2 regularization parameter (alpha). If these aren't well-calibrated, the model can easily overfit or underfit.

No Hierarchical Learning: ELMs don't learn hierarchical features like deep networks do. For highly structured data like text or images, they won't cut it—but for tabular financial data and smooth mathematical functions, they are an absolute cheat code.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: AutoScientist-Quant: Can AI Actually Automate the Quant Desk?

We have all heard the pitch: "We have plugged an LLM into our data feed, and it is printing money." But if you have ever actually tried to get an LLM to generate trading signals (alphas), you will know it is usually a recipe for massive API bills and strategies that look like Renaissance Technologies in backtests but look like a dumpster fire in production. A paper from Google and the University of Cambridge, titled "AutoScientist-Quant: Self-Evolving Coding Agents for Automatic Research in Quantitative Investment" (August 2026), takes a massive, beautifully cynical wrench to this entire space.
Why this paper is worth your time

Most academic papers on "AI alpha" are, frankly, a bit of a joke. They suffer from what we in the trade call "lookahead bias"—the AI accidentally peeks at the test data during its feedback loop, essentially memorising the exam answers. This paper is different. The authors did not just build a new AI agent; they went through existing academic pipelines with a fine-tooth comb, found the bugs where the AI was cheating, and fixed them. What is left is a highly realistic, end-to-end framework that treats quantitative research not as a magic trick, but as a budget-constrained engineering problem.
The core idea: End-to-end automation under a budget

Existing LLM quant tools usually stop at generating a mathematical formula. They leave the annoying bits—like choosing which machine learning library to use (XGBoost, LightGBM, PyTorch), tuning the hyperparameters, and managing transaction costs—to human coders. AutoScientist-Quant automates the whole lot. It uses a single "controller" agent that manages a strict compute budget. At each turn, it looks at how much budget is left and decides whether to:

items: Improve: Refine an existing alpha idea that shows promise.
Combine: Merge two separate ideas to see if they create a stronger signal.
Pivot: Abandon a dead-end path and try a completely new hypothesis.
Stop: Call it a day and deploy the strategy before burning more cash.

content.text: The silent killer: Lookahead bias

The most satisfying part of this paper is the authors' absolute refusal to play the usual academic hype games. They point out that many existing AI quant papers show spectacular backtest results because of subtle data leakage. When they fixed these lookahead issues and kept the feedback window strictly disjoint from the test window, the baseline AI models' returns collapsed. In fact, one popular baseline, QuantaAlpha, went from looking brilliant to delivering a -0.2% annualised excess return once transaction costs and turnover were properly priced in. Ouch.

The search cannot adapt during the run, automation usually ends at alpha generation while library selection and model choice stay manual, and alpha discovery can read the test window through loop feedback or code problems.
The results

When tested on Chinese equity universes (CSI 300, 500, 800, and 1000), AutoScientist-Quant consistently outperformed other agentic frameworks. On the CSI 300 index using the standard ALPHA158 dataset, it achieved an Information Coefficient (IC) of 0.034 and an Information Ratio of 0.500. Crucially, it translated this into a positive annualised excess return of 3.5% after accounting for transaction costs and turnover. It also kept the smallest maximum drawdown among all tested agents.
How to use this at work or in interviews

items: In interviews: If you are interviewing for a quant or buy-side role, bringing up this paper shows you understand the difference between "paper alpha" and "production alpha". You can talk about how most LLM-based signal generation suffers from lookahead bias because the feedback loop accidentally peeks at the test window, and how end-to-end automation must include model selection and library tuning, not just formula generation.

At the pub / with colleagues: It is a great talking point about the reality of AI in finance. The bottleneck is not the LLM's intelligence; it is the rigor of the sandbox we build for it. If you do not bound the agent with a budget-aware search tree and strict data boundaries, it will either bankrupt you on API costs or cheat by overfitting.

content.text: What to skim vs. what to read

If you are short on time, skip the heavy math in Section 3 regarding the exact formulation of the rank metrics. Instead, focus on Section 2 to understand how the controller agent manages the search tree, and Section 4's tables. The contrast between the information metrics (which look great for everyone) and the actual portfolio returns (where the baselines fall off a cliff due to transaction costs) is a masterclass in why backtesting is hard.

content.text: The Foot-in-the-Door Technique: Winning Big by Asking Small

Imagine you are trying to convince a notoriously defensive, risk-averse Chief Risk Officer to let your team use a new, cutting-edge AI tool for portfolio optimization. If you walk into their office with a 50-page proposal demanding a complete overhaul of the firm's compliance infrastructure and a six-figure budget, you will be laughed straight out of the room. Instead, you need a classic psychological lever: the Foot-in-the-Door (FITD) technique.

First formally documented in 1966 by Stanford psychologists Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser, the FITD technique is a compliance tactic that involves getting a person to agree to a large request by first having them agree to a modest, almost trivial one. In their famous study, researchers asked homeowners to place a tiny, unobtrusive three-inch sign reading 'Be a safe driver' in their window. Nearly everyone agreed. A couple of weeks later, a different researcher asked those same homeowners to erect a massive, ugly billboard on their front lawns that blocked the view of their house. Amazingly, 76% of those who had accepted the tiny sign agreed to the giant billboard, compared to only 17% of a control group who were asked for the billboard outright.

Why does this work? It boils down to self-perception theory. Humans have an innate psychological drive to remain consistent with their past actions. Once someone agrees to a small request, their internal narrative shifts: 'I am the kind of person who supports this initiative.' When the larger request comes later, refusing it would create cognitive dissonance. They comply to maintain their self-image.
How It Plays Out in the City
In investment banking, asset management, and corporate life, we often try to swing for the fences on the first pitch, only to get shut down. FITD is the antidote. Consider these scenarios:

items: The Client Pitch: Instead of asking a prospective institutional client to reallocate 10% of their entire portfolio to your fund on day one, ask them to let you run a complimentary backtest on a tiny, non-core slice of their historical data. Once they say yes and engage with your team, they have psychologically 'opted in' to your process, making the eventual mandate pitch infinitely easier.

The Internal Project: Want to implement a complex new quantitative risk model? Don't ask for a full migration. Ask the head of trading if you can run the model in parallel on just one minor, low-volume book for two weeks, purely for 'shadow observation'. Once they agree and see it working, expanding it to the rest of the desk is a natural next step.

Managing Upwards: If you want your MD to sponsor your promotion or back a highly controversial investment thesis, don't drop a massive, high-stakes decision on their desk. Start by asking for a quick five-minute coffee to get their 'expert advice' on one specific, minor aspect of the thesis. Once they've given advice, they are co-authors of the idea and will naturally defend the larger thesis later.

content.text: How to Use It This Week

To execute this effectively without looking manipulative, follow three simple rules. First, make the initial request genuinely easy to say yes to—it should require minimal effort, time, or political capital. Second, ensure the small request is directly connected to the ultimate goal; agreeing to buy cupcakes for the office charity drive won't help you get a budget approved for a Python library. Third, leave a natural buffer of a few days or weeks between the small 'yes' and the big ask, allowing their self-perception to crystallise.
If you want to move a mountain, don't start by ordering the digger. Ask if you can borrow a shovel to clear a single path.
